# shared_thread - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/shared_thread/

## Expand description

This crate provides [ SharedThread](https://docs.rs/struct.SharedThread.html), a wrapper around

[that lets multiple threads wait on a shared thread and read its output, with an optional timeout.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/struct.JoinHandle.html)

`std::thread::JoinHandle`For example code, see [the  SharedThread example](https://docs.rs/struct.SharedThread.html#example).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Shared](https://docs.rs/struct.SharedThread.html)- Thread
- A wrapper around `std::thread::JoinHandle`

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

Vue compiler for DOM platform.

This module provides DOM-specific compilation including:

- DOM element and attribute validation
- v-model transforms for form elements
- v-on event modifiers

# vize_atelier_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/vize_atelier_core/0.273.0/vize_atelier_core/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#vize_atelier_core)vize_atelier_core

Atelier Core - The core workshop for Vize. Vue template transforms and code generation.

[§](https://docs.rs#name-origin)Name Origin

**Atelier** (/ˌætəlˈjeɪ/) is an artist’s workshop or studio where creative work
is produced. The “core” atelier is the foundational workshop where the essential
Vue template processing happens - transforming and code generation.
`vize_atelier_core` provides the foundational infrastructure
that all other Vize compilers build upon.

# distributed_cli - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/distributed_cli/2.3.3/distributed_cli/

## Expand description

The `dctl` CLI for Distributed services — both a binary and a library.

It bundles two things in one crate so there is no cross-repo coordination:

- **Pure generation**(the [- `generate`]/[- `atlas`] modules): the rules for a Distributed service project — Cargo layout, Rust source templates, manifest wiring, GitOps/Knative inference, GitHub workflows, and Atlas schema resources. These perform no I/O —- `generate_service_scaffold`- `ServiceScaffoldSpec`- `GeneratedProject`- `render_atlas_schema`- `AtlasSchema`.
- **The command surface**(the [- `cli`] module): the clap types and- `run`- `gh`, compiling the manifest harness).

The `dctl` binary parses [ ServiceArgs](https://docs.rs/struct.ServiceArgs.html) and calls

[. Another CLI (e.g.](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html)

`run``hops`) can depend on this crate, mount [under its own subcommand, and dispatch with](https://docs.rs/struct.ServiceArgs.html)

`ServiceArgs`[— re-exporting the commands rather than reimplementing them.](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html)

`run`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# vize_croquis - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/vize_croquis/0.273.0/vize_croquis/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#vize_croquis)vize_croquis

Croquis - The semantic analysis layer for Vize.

[§](https://docs.rs#name-origin)Name Origin

**Croquis** (/kʁɔ.ki/) is a French term for a quick, sketchy drawing that captures
the essential features of a subject. Like how artists use croquis to rapidly
capture the essence of a pose or scene, `vize_croquis` quickly analyzes Vue
templates to extract semantic meaning from the syntactic structure.

[§](https://docs.rs#purpose)Purpose

This crate bridges the gap between parsing (vize_armature) and transformation (vize_atelier_core) by providing:

- **Scope Analysis**: Track variable scopes across templates and scripts
- **Binding Resolution**: Resolve identifiers to their declarations
- **Reactivity Tracking**: Understand ref/reactive dependencies
- **Symbol Tables**: Fast lookup of bindings and their metadata

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

```
vize_armature (Parse)
       ↓
  vize_relief (AST)
       ↓
 vize_croquis (Semantic Analysis)  ← This crate
       ↓
vize_atelier_core (Transform)
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use analyzer::`- [Analyzer](https://docs.rs/drawer/struct.Drawer.html);
- `pub use analyzer::`- [AnalyzerOptions](https://docs.rs/drawer/struct.DrawerOptions.html);
- `pub use croquis::`- [AnalysisStats](https://docs.rs/croquis/type.AnalysisStats.html);

- `pub use croquis::`- [COMPILER_MACRO_NAMES](https://docs.rs/croquis/constant.COMPILER_MACRO_NAMES.html);
- `pub use croquis::`- [ComponentShape](https://docs.rs/croquis/enum.ComponentShape.html);
- `pub use croquis::`- [Croquis](https://docs.rs/croquis/struct.Croquis.html);
- `pub use croquis::`- [CroquisStats](https://docs.rs/croquis/struct.CroquisStats.html);
- `pub use croquis::`- [ImportStatementInfo](https://docs.rs/croquis/struct.ImportStatementInfo.html);

# vize_armature - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/vize_armature/0.273.0/vize_armature/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#vize_armature)vize_armature

Armature - The structural parser framework for Vize. Vue template tokenizer and parser implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#name-origin)Name Origin

**Armature** (/ˈɑːrmətʃər/) is the internal skeleton or framework that supports
a sculpture during its creation. Similarly, `vize_armature` provides the parsing
framework that builds the AST structure defined in `vize_relief`.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- High-performance HTML tokenizer optimized for Vue templates
- State machine-based parsing
- Full Vue directive and interpolation support
- Error recovery and detailed error reporting

# vize_relief - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/vize_relief/0.273.0/vize_relief/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#vize_relief)vize_relief

Relief - The sculptured AST surface for Vize. Vue template Abstract Syntax Tree definitions, errors, and compiler options.

[§](https://docs.rs#name-origin)Name Origin

**Relief** (/rɪˈliːf/) is a sculptural technique where figures project from a flat
background, creating depth and dimension. Like how relief carving reveals forms
from a surface, `vize_relief` defines the structural forms (AST nodes) that
represent Vue template syntax.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- Complete Vue template AST node definitions
- Compiler error types and codes
- Parser, transform, and codegen options
- Arena-allocated nodes for zero-copy JavaScript interop
- Serialization support with serde

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# vize_carton - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/vize_carton/0.273.0/vize_carton/

## Expand description

Carton - The artist’s toolbox for Vize.

This crate provides the foundational utilities and data structures for the Vize compiler, much like a carton (artist’s portfolio case) holds all the essential tools and materials an artist needs for their work.

[§](https://docs.rs#modules)Modules

- **Allocator**: Arena-based memory allocation for efficient AST construction
- **Shared utilities**: DOM configuration, optimization flags, and helper functions
- **Telegraph**: Generic message fan-out for report emitters

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use vize_carton::{Allocator, Box, Vec};
let allocator = Allocator::default();
// Allocate a boxed value
let boxed = Box::new_in(42, allocator.as_bump());
assert_eq!(*boxed, 42);
// Create a vector
let mut vec = Vec::new_in(allocator.as_bump());
vec.push(1);
vec.push(2);
vec.push(3);
assert_eq!(vec.len(), 3);
```

# privacy_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/privacy-core/0.1.4/privacy_core/

## Expand description

privacy-core — shared, halo2-free foundation for the privacy-indexer and privacy-relayer.

Contains only the light, proving-stack-free pieces both services need:

- `ethereum`— event-log decode + bundle/erc/finalize calldata encode (ethabi).
- `types`— plain serde data structures (stored bundle, indexed notes/bundles).
- `intent`— BTC shield-intent helpers (single-sig federation V1).

The Fr/circuit/witness machinery (proving, note decryption, key derivation, Poseidon) deliberately stays out of this crate so the services don’t pull in halo2.

# meerkat_runtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/meerkat-runtime/0.7.12/meerkat_runtime/

## Expand description

meerkat-runtime — v9 runtime control-plane for Meerkat agent lifecycle.

This crate implements the runtime/control-plane layer of the v9 Canonical
Lifecycle specification. It sits between surfaces (CLI, RPC, REST, MCP)
and core (`meerkat-core`), managing:

- Input acceptance, validation, and queueing
- InputState lifecycle tracking
- Policy resolution (what to do with each input)
- Runtime state machine (Initializing ↔ Idle ↔ Attached ↔ Running ↔ Retired/Stopped/Destroyed)
- Retire/recycle/reset lifecycle operations
- RuntimeEvent observability

Core-facing types (RunPrimitive, RunEvent, CoreExecutor, etc.) live in
`meerkat-core::lifecycle`. This crate contains everything else.

# hanzo-kernel

**Write a GPU kernel once in Rust. Run it on CUDA, ROCm, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU, and CPU — at or above hand-tuned speed.**

```
use *;
```
That is the whole kernel. It lowers to native SPIR-V, PTX, HIP, and MSL — no per-backend rewrite, no shading-language dialect, no `unsafe` FFI.

## Why

A production inference stack hand-writes the same ~20 operations four times — once per backend, in four languages (CUDA C++, Metal Shading Language, HIP C++, GLSL). That Cartesian product isn't just a maintenance tax; it is where the bugs breed, because **one operation with four implementations has four numeric behaviors.** A model that generates coherently on Metal can collapse into repetition on CUDA — same weights, same math, different rounding in a hand-tuned kernel.

`hanzo-kernel` collapses the **product** into a **sum**: `backends × types × ops` → `backends + types + ops`. One Rust source per operation, lowered everywhere. Uniform numeric behavior stops being something you chase with four test suites and becomes a structural property of a single source.

## The claim, measured

Portability usually means a performance downgrade. It doesn't here. Every number below is measured, bit-exact-gated against a CPU oracle, and reproducible with the bundled `matvec-check` binary.

| Kernel | Backend | Result |
|---|---|---|
| int8 dp4a matvec | Vulkan (AMD gfx1151) | 196 GB/s — 118% of the hand-tuned kernel it replaces |
| int8 dp4a matvec | Metal (Apple M4 Max) | 206 GB/s |
| `rms_norm` | Vulkan, in the live engine | 10.6× the hand-written kernelit replaced (now deleted) |
| `softmax` | Vulkan, in the live engine | 351 GB/s (replaced the hand-written kernel) |
| all ops | CPU / Vulkan / Metal | bit-exact from one source(max_rel ≤ 1e-3) |

The `dot` on a `Line<i8>` lowers to a single `OpSDot` on Vulkan (verified in the emitted SPIR-V binary) — the *same* hardware integer-dot instruction the hand-written kernels use, 2.35× a scalar loop. The DSL doesn't emulate the fast path; it reaches it.

## Install

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
Pick your backend with a feature flag (drop `cpu` for GPU-only builds — it pulls an LLVM/MLIR toolchain):

```
# GPU-only, no CPU toolchain
 = {  = "0.2",  = false,  = ["vulkan"] }
```
| Feature | Backend |
|---|---|
| `cpu`(default) | CPU reference runtime — the bit-exact oracle |
| `vulkan` | Vulkan (SPIR-V) — AMD, Intel, NVIDIA |
| `metal` | Metal (MSL) — Apple Silicon |
| `cuda` | CUDA (PTX/NVRTC) — NVIDIA |
| `rocm` | ROCm (HIP) — AMD |

## The surface

Three attributes and two nouns — named for what they are, not for a framework.

- `#[kernel(targets(...))]`— a launch entry point.- `targets(...)`is validated at compile time (an unknown backend is a compile error) and self-documents where the kernel runs.
- `#[device]`— an on-GPU helper function, inlined into a kernel. A kernel is- *launched*; a device function is a- *piece*of one.
- `Grid`/- `Block`— the launch shape: the grid of thread blocks, and the block of threads.
- `Array`,- `Float`,- `Line`— the data. Already the simple, accurate words.

Every performance primitive is a first-class part of the surface and lowers to the native instruction:

| Primitive | Lowers to |
|---|---|
| `Line<i8>::dot` | `dp4a`/`OpSDotAccSat`(int8 4-way dot) |
| `cmma` | tensor cores (WMMA / cooperative-matrix / simdgroup) |
| `plane_sum`,`plane_broadcast` | subgroup / warp reduce & shuffle |
| `SharedMemory`,`Atomic`, barriers | native shared memory, atomics, sync |

## Built-in op library

Reusable, bit-exact kernels — not toys. Each ships with a CPU oracle and a bit-exact gate.

- `quant`- `matvec_q8`,- `matvec_q4k`(in-kernel K-quant decode), dp4a matvec (- `_blk`block-per-row +- `_sg`subgroup variants), packed-Q8_0 decode with in-kernel fp16 unpack.
- `norm`- `rms_norm`,- `layer_norm`,- `add_rmsnorm`(fused, multi-output).
- `rope`- `rope_half`(GPT-NeoX) and- `rope_interleaved`(GPT-J) conventions.
- `attn`- `sdpa`and- `sdpa_runtime`: GQA + online (flash-style) softmax with a runtime-length KV cache. One stable attention implementation across backends — the structural cure for repetition-collapse.

Run the correctness + throughput gate yourself:

```
```
## Design

Four ideas, borrowed from Rich Hickey and applied to kernels:

- **Decomplect.**Ops, quantization types, and backends are three orthogonal axes braided together in hand-written code. Pulled apart, they compose — you write each axis once.- `backends × types × ops`becomes- `backends + types + ops`.
- **Values, not places.**- [CubeCL](https://github.com/tracel-ai/cubecl)is the lowering engine — the implementation- *value*.- `hanzo_kernel`is the stable- *namespace*you build against; the string- `cubecl`appears in exactly one line of one- `Cargo.toml`. The engine can be upgraded or vendored without touching a kernel.
- **One numeric behavior.**A single source means a single rounding path. The "coherent on Metal, collapsed on CUDA" class of bug cannot occur — not because four copies were tested into agreement, but because there is one copy.
- **Perf-gated migration, never a downgrade.**A hand-tuned kernel is retired for its DSL twin- **only**when the twin is bit-exact- *and*at least as fast. Where a hand-tuned kernel still wins, it stays as the peak path and the DSL is the portable fallback for backends that lack it. Coverage always grows; speed never regresses.

## Status

Published and in production. `rms_norm` and `softmax` are live DSL kernels in the [Hanzo ML](https://github.com/hanzoai/ml) inference engine — their hand-written predecessors are deleted. The full op library is bit-exact on CPU, Vulkan, and Metal, and shelf-ready for the backends still on hand-tuned kernels. A generated DSL kernel dispatches through the engine's real Vulkan and Metal pipelines with `maxerr = 0` — the DSL plugs in as a **code generator**, not a second runtime.

[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! For example code, see [the `SharedThread` example](struct.SharedThread.html#example).
[6](https://docs.rs#6)
[7](https://docs.rs#7)#![deny(unsafe_code)]
[8](https://docs.rs#8)

[18](https://docs.rs#18)/// A wrapper around [`std::thread::JoinHandle`] that allows for multiple waiters.
[19](https://docs.rs#19)///
[20](https://docs.rs#20)/// The high-level differences between `SharedThread` and [`JoinHandle`] are:
[21](https://docs.rs#21)///
[22](https://docs.rs#22)/// - [`join`][SharedThread::join] takes `&self` rather than `&mut self`.
[23](https://docs.rs#23)/// - [`join`][SharedThread::join] returns `&T` rather than `T`. For taking ownership of `T`, see
[24](https://docs.rs#24)///   [`into_output`][SharedThread::into_output].
[25](https://docs.rs#25)/// - `SharedThread` also provides [`join_timeout`][Self::join_timeout],
[26](https://docs.rs#26)///   [`join_deadline`][Self::join_deadline], and [`try_join`][SharedThread::try_join].
[27](https://docs.rs#27)/// - Rather than converting panics in into
[28](https://docs.rs#28)///   [`std::thread::Result`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/type.Result.html), which usually
[29](https://docs.rs#29)///   requires the caller to `.unwrap()` every `.join()`, `SharedThread` propagates panics
[30](https://docs.rs#30)///   automatically.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)///
[32](https://docs.rs#32)/// # Example
[33](https://docs.rs#33)///
[34](https://docs.rs#34)/// ```
[35](https://docs.rs#35)/// use shared_thread::SharedThread;
[36](https://docs.rs#36)/// use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering::Relaxed};
[37](https://docs.rs#37)///
[38](https://docs.rs#38)/// // Use this flag to tell our shared thread when to stop.
[39](https://docs.rs#39)/// static EXIT_FLAG: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(false);
[40](https://docs.rs#40)///
[41](https://docs.rs#41)/// // Start a background thread that we'll share with several waiting threads.
[42](https://docs.rs#42)/// let shared_thread = SharedThread::spawn(|| {
[43](https://docs.rs#43)///     // Pretend this is some expensive, useful background work...
[44](https://docs.rs#44)///     while (!EXIT_FLAG.load(Relaxed)) {}
[45](https://docs.rs#45)///
[46](https://docs.rs#46)///     42
[47](https://docs.rs#47)/// });
[48](https://docs.rs#48)///
[49](https://docs.rs#49)/// // It's up to you how to share the SharedThread object with other threads. In this sense it's
[50](https://docs.rs#50)/// // like any other object you might need to share, like say a HashMap or a File. The common
[51](https://docs.rs#51)/// // options are to put it in an Arc, or to let "scoped" threads borrow it directly. Let's use
[52](https://docs.rs#52)/// // scoped threads.
[53](https://docs.rs#53)/// std::thread::scope(|scope| {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)///     // Spawn three waiter threads that each wait on the shared thread.
[55](https://docs.rs#55)///     let waiter1 = scope.spawn(|| shared_thread.join());
[56](https://docs.rs#56)///     let waiter2 = scope.spawn(|| shared_thread.join());
[57](https://docs.rs#57)///     let waiter3 = scope.spawn(|| shared_thread.join());
[58](https://docs.rs#58)///
[59](https://docs.rs#59)///     // In this example, the shared thread is going to keep looping until we set the EXIT_FLAG.
[60](https://docs.rs#60)///     // In the meantime, .is_finished() returns false, and .try_join() returns None.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)///     assert!(!shared_thread.is_finished());
[62](https://docs.rs#62)///     assert_eq!(shared_thread.try_join(), None);
[63](https://docs.rs#63)///
[64](https://docs.rs#64)///     // Ask the shared thread to stop looping.
[65](https://docs.rs#65)///     EXIT_FLAG.store(true, Relaxed);
[66](https://docs.rs#66)///
[67](https://docs.rs#67)///     // Now all the calls to .join() above will return quickly, and each of the waiter threads
[68](https://docs.rs#68)///     // will get a reference to the shared thread's output, &42.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)///     assert_eq!(*waiter1.join().unwrap(), 42);
[70](https://docs.rs#70)///     assert_eq!(*waiter2.join().unwrap(), 42);
[71](https://docs.rs#71)///     assert_eq!(*waiter3.join().unwrap(), 42);
[72](https://docs.rs#72)///
[73](https://docs.rs#73)///     // Now that the shared thread has finished, .is_finished() returns true, and .try_join()
[74](https://docs.rs#74)///     // returns Some(&42).
[75](https://docs.rs#75)///     assert!(shared_thread.is_finished());
[76](https://docs.rs#76)///     assert_eq!(*shared_thread.try_join().unwrap(), 42);
[77](https://docs.rs#77)/// });
[78](https://docs.rs#78)///
[79](https://docs.rs#79)///  // We can take ownership of the output by consuming the SharedThread object. As with any
[80](https://docs.rs#80)///  // non-Copy type in Rust, this requires that the SharedThread is not borrowed.
[81](https://docs.rs#81)///  assert_eq!(shared_thread.into_output(), 42);
[82](https://docs.rs#82)/// ```
[83](https://docs.rs#83)///
[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// [`std::thread::JoinHandle`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/struct.JoinHandle.html
[85](https://docs.rs#85)/// [`JoinHandle`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/struct.JoinHandle.html
[86](https://docs.rs#86)#[derive(Debug)]
[87](https://docs.rs#87)pub struct SharedThread<T> {
[88](https://docs.rs#88)    state: Mutex<State<T>>,
[89](https://docs.rs#89)    exit_signal: Arc<ExitSignal>,
[90](https://docs.rs#90)    output: OnceLock<T>,
[91](https://docs.rs#91)}
[92](https://docs.rs#92)
[93](https://docs.rs#93)// The shared thread sets this bool to true and signals the condvar when it exits, even if it
[94](https://docs.rs#94)// panicks.
[95](https://docs.rs#95)#[derive(Debug)]
[96](https://docs.rs#96)struct ExitSignal {
[97](https://docs.rs#97)    mutex: Mutex<bool>,
[98](https://docs.rs#98)    condvar: Condvar,
[99](https://docs.rs#99)}
[100](https://docs.rs#100)
[101](https://docs.rs#101)enum State<T> {
[102](https://docs.rs#102)    Running(thread::JoinHandle<T>),
[103](https://docs.rs#103)    // Note that the return value T goes in the OnceLock. If it lived here in the Exited variant,
[104](https://docs.rs#104)    // it would be stuck inside the state Mutex, and we couldn't share it with simple references.
[105](https://docs.rs#105)    Exited,
[106](https://docs.rs#106)    Panicked,
[107](https://docs.rs#107)}
[108](https://docs.rs#108)
[109](https://docs.rs#109)use State::*;
[110](https://docs.rs#110)
[111](https://docs.rs#111)impl<T> fmt::Debug for State<T> {
[112](https://docs.rs#112)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
[113](https://docs.rs#113)        match self {
[114](https://docs.rs#114)            Running { .. } => write!(f, "Running"),
[115](https://docs.rs#115)            Exited => write!(f, "Exited"),
[116](https://docs.rs#116)            Panicked => write!(f, "Panicked"),
[117](https://docs.rs#117)        }
[118](https://docs.rs#118)    }
[119](https://docs.rs#119)}
[120](https://docs.rs#120)
[121](https://docs.rs#121)impl<T: Send + 'static> SharedThread<T> {
[122](https://docs.rs#122)    /// Spawn a new `SharedThread`.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    ///
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    /// # Panics
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    ///
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    /// This function calls
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    /// [`std::thread::spawn`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/fn.spawn.html) internally,
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    /// which panics if it fails to spawn a thread.
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    pub fn spawn<F>(f: F) -> Self
[130](https://docs.rs#130)    where
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        F: FnOnce() -> T + Send + 'static,
[132](https://docs.rs#132)    {
[133](https://docs.rs#133)        let exit_signal = Arc::new(ExitSignal {
[134](https://docs.rs#134)            mutex: Mutex::new(false),
[135](https://docs.rs#135)            condvar: Condvar::new(),
[136](https://docs.rs#136)        });
[137](https://docs.rs#137)        let exit_signal_clone = Arc::clone(&exit_signal);
[138](https://docs.rs#138)        let handle = thread::spawn(move || {
[139](https://docs.rs#139)            // Whether or not the closure `f` panics, set the exited flag and notify the condvar.
[140](https://docs.rs#140)            // It's not clear to me that the concept of "unwind safety" in the standard library was
[141](https://docs.rs#141)            // a good indea, but at least it doesn't require any unsafe code to work around it.
[142](https://docs.rs#142)            let unwind_result = catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(f));
[143](https://docs.rs#143)            let mut guard = lock_ignoring_poison(&exit_signal_clone.mutex);
[144](https://docs.rs#144)            *guard = true;
[145](https://docs.rs#145)            exit_signal_clone.condvar.notify_all();
[146](https://docs.rs#146)            // Now that we've signaled exit, if there was a panic, propagate it. The first waiter
[147](https://docs.rs#147)            // thread will observe it. (Subsequent waiter threads will only see the Panicked state
[148](https://docs.rs#148)            // variant.)
[149](https://docs.rs#149)            match unwind_result {
[150](https://docs.rs#150)                Ok(return_value) => return_value,
[151](https://docs.rs#151)                Err(panic) => resume_unwind(panic),
[152](https://docs.rs#152)            }
[153](https://docs.rs#153)        });
[154](https://docs.rs#154)        SharedThread {
[155](https://docs.rs#155)            state: Mutex::new(Running(handle)),
[156](https://docs.rs#156)            exit_signal,
[157](https://docs.rs#157)            output: OnceLock::new(),
[158](https://docs.rs#158)        }
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    }
[160](https://docs.rs#160)}
[161](https://docs.rs#161)
[162](https://docs.rs#162)// A thread that multiple other threads can wait on simultaneously.
[163](https://docs.rs#163)impl<T> SharedThread<T> {
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    fn join_exited_thread(&self, exit_signal_guard: MutexGuard<bool>) -> &T {
[165](https://docs.rs#165)        // It's not really important that we pass down the exit_signal_guard here, but it would
[166](https://docs.rs#166)        // probably live across this call anway, so it seems cleaner to take ownership of it.
[167](https://docs.rs#167)        debug_assert!(*exit_signal_guard, "the thread exited");
[168](https://docs.rs#168)
[169](https://docs.rs#169)        let mut state_guard = lock_ignoring_poison(&self.state);
[170](https://docs.rs#170)        match &*state_guard {
[171](https://docs.rs#171)            // Running means we're the thread that needs to .join(). Fall through.
[172](https://docs.rs#172)            Running(_) => {}
[173](https://docs.rs#173)            // Exited or Panicked means someone already joined.
[174](https://docs.rs#174)            Exited => return self.output.get().unwrap(),
[175](https://docs.rs#175)            Panicked => panic!("shared thread panicked"),
[176](https://docs.rs#176)        };
[177](https://docs.rs#177)
[178](https://docs.rs#178)        // We need to .join(), so take the JoinHandle by value. Use the Panicked state as a
[179](https://docs.rs#179)        // placeholder, so that it's the state we leave behind if something does in fact panic.
[180](https://docs.rs#180)        // This makes the Panicked state kind of ambiguous between "the other thread panicked" or
[181](https://docs.rs#181)        // "we failed an assert somewhere", but at least the initial panic backtrace will make it
[182](https://docs.rs#182)        // clear what happened.
[183](https://docs.rs#183)        let Running(handle) = mem::replace(&mut *state_guard, Panicked) else {
[184](https://docs.rs#184)            unreachable!()
[185](https://docs.rs#185)        };
[186](https://docs.rs#186)
[187](https://docs.rs#187)        // The thread has signaled that it's exiting, so .join() will return quickly. (It might
[188](https://docs.rs#188)        // block briefly it the thread is still cleaning itself up.) If it panicked, propagate the
[189](https://docs.rs#189)        // panic.
[190](https://docs.rs#190)        match handle.join() {
[191](https://docs.rs#191)            Ok(return_value) => {
[192](https://docs.rs#192)                // Because we set `output` while we hold the state mutex, it's guaranteed that
[193](https://docs.rs#193)                // subsequent threads that see the Exited state will also see that `output` is set.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)                let set_result = self.output.set(return_value);
[195](https://docs.rs#195)                assert!(set_result.is_ok(), "output must be previously unset");
[196](https://docs.rs#196)                *state_guard = Exited;
[197](https://docs.rs#197)                self.output.get().unwrap()
[198](https://docs.rs#198)            }
[199](https://docs.rs#199)            Err(panic) => resume_unwind(panic),
[200](https://docs.rs#200)        }
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    }
[202](https://docs.rs#202)
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    /// Wait for the shared thread to finish, then return `&T`. This blocks the current thread.
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    ///
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    /// # Panics
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    ///
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    /// This function panics if the shared thread panicked. The original panic is propagated
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    /// directly with [`resume_unwind`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/panic/fn.resume_unwind.html)
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    /// the first time. Subsequent calls panic with a generic message.
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    pub fn join(&self) -> &T {
[211](https://docs.rs#211)        let mut exit_signal_guard = lock_ignoring_poison(&self.exit_signal.mutex);
[212](https://docs.rs#212)        while !*exit_signal_guard {
[213](https://docs.rs#213)            exit_signal_guard = wait_ignoring_poison(&self.exit_signal.condvar, exit_signal_guard);
[214](https://docs.rs#214)        }
[215](https://docs.rs#215)        self.join_exited_thread(exit_signal_guard)
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    }
[217](https://docs.rs#217)
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    /// Wait with a timeout for the shared thread to finish. If it finishes in time (or it already
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    /// finished), return `Some(&T)`, otherwise return `None`. This blocks the current thread.
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    ///
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    /// # Panics
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    ///
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    /// This function panics if the shared thread panicked. The original panic is propagated
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// directly with [`resume_unwind`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/panic/fn.resume_unwind.html)
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    /// the first time it's observed. Subsequent calls panic with a generic message.
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    pub fn join_timeout(&self, timeout: Duration) -> Option<&T> {
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        let deadline = Instant::now() + timeout;
[228](https://docs.rs#228)        self.join_deadline(deadline)
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    }
[230](https://docs.rs#230)
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    /// Wait with a deadline for the shared thread to finish. If it finishes in time (or it already
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// finished), return `Some(&T)`, otherwise return `None`. This blocks the current thread.
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    ///
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    /// # Panics
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    ///
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    /// This function panics if the shared thread panicked. The original panic is propagated
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    /// directly with [`resume_unwind`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/panic/fn.resume_unwind.html)
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    /// the first time it's observed. Subsequent calls panic with a generic message.
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    pub fn join_deadline(&self, deadline: Instant) -> Option<&T> {
[240](https://docs.rs#240)        let mut exit_signal_guard = lock_ignoring_poison(&self.exit_signal.mutex);
[241](https://docs.rs#241)        while !*exit_signal_guard {
[242](https://docs.rs#242)            if Instant::now() > deadline {
[243](https://docs.rs#243)                return None;
[244](https://docs.rs#244)            }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)            exit_signal_guard = wait_deadline_ignoring_poison(
[246](https://docs.rs#246)                &self.exit_signal.condvar,
[247](https://docs.rs#247)                exit_signal_guard,
[248](https://docs.rs#248)                deadline,
[249](https://docs.rs#249)            );
[250](https://docs.rs#250)        }
[251](https://docs.rs#251)        Some(self.join_exited_thread(exit_signal_guard))
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    }
[253](https://docs.rs#253)
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    /// Return `Some(&T)` if the shared thread has already finished, otherwise `None`. This always
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    /// returns quickly.
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    ///
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    /// # Panics
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    ///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    /// This function panics if the shared thread panicked. The original panic is propagated
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    /// directly with [`resume_unwind`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/panic/fn.resume_unwind.html)
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    /// the first time it's observed. Subsequent calls panic with a generic message.
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    pub fn try_join(&self) -> Option<&T> {
[263](https://docs.rs#263)        let exit_signal_guard = lock_ignoring_poison(&self.exit_signal.mutex);
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        if *exit_signal_guard {
[265](https://docs.rs#265)            Some(self.join_exited_thread(exit_signal_guard))
[266](https://docs.rs#266)        } else {
[267](https://docs.rs#267)            None
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        }
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    }
[270](https://docs.rs#270)
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    /// Wait for the shared thread to finish, then return `T`. This blocks the current. This
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    /// requires ownership of the `SharedThread` and consumes it.
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    ///
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    /// # Panics
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    ///
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    /// This function panics if the shared thread panicked. The original panic is propagated
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// directly with [`resume_unwind`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/panic/fn.resume_unwind.html)
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    /// the first time it's observed. Subsequent calls panic with a generic message.
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    pub fn into_output(self) -> T {
[280](https://docs.rs#280)        self.join();
[281](https://docs.rs#281)        self.output.into_inner().expect("should be set")
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    }
[283](https://docs.rs#283)
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    /// Return `true` if the shared thread has finished, `false` otherwise.
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    ///
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    /// This function never blocks. If it returns `true`, [`try_join`][Self::try_join],
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    /// [`join_timeout`][Self::join_timeout], and [`join_deadline`][Self::join_deadline] are
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    /// guaranteed not to return `None`, and all join functions are guaranteed to return quickly.
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    pub fn is_finished(&self) -> bool {
[290](https://docs.rs#290)        *lock_ignoring_poison(&self.exit_signal.mutex)
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    }
[292](https://docs.rs#292)}
[293](https://docs.rs#293)
[294](https://docs.rs#294)fn lock_ignoring_poison<T>(mutex: &Mutex<T>) -> MutexGuard<'_, T> {
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    match mutex.lock() {
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        Ok(guard) => guard,
[297](https://docs.rs#297)        Err(e) => e.into_inner(),
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    }
[299](https://docs.rs#299)}
[300](https://docs.rs#300)
[301](https://docs.rs#301)fn wait_ignoring_poison<'guard, T>(
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    condvar: &Condvar,
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    guard: MutexGuard<'guard, T>,
[304](https://docs.rs#304)) -> MutexGuard<'guard, T> {
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    match condvar.wait(guard) {
[306](https://docs.rs#306)        Ok(guard) => guard,
[307](https://docs.rs#307)        Err(e) => e.into_inner(),
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    }
[309](https://docs.rs#309)}
[310](https://docs.rs#310)
[311](https://docs.rs#311)fn wait_deadline_ignoring_poison<'guard, T>(
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    condvar: &Condvar,
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    guard: MutexGuard<'guard, T>,
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    deadline: Instant,
[315](https://docs.rs#315)) -> MutexGuard<'guard, T> {
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    let timeout = deadline.saturating_duration_since(Instant::now());
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    match condvar.wait_timeout(guard, timeout) {
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        Ok((guard, _)) => guard,
[319](https://docs.rs#319)        Err(e) => e.into_inner().0,
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    }
[321](https://docs.rs#321)}

[323](https://docs.rs#323)#[cfg(test)]
[324](https://docs.rs#324)mod test {
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    use super::*;
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering::Relaxed};
[327](https://docs.rs#327)
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    #[test]
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    fn test_join_and_try_join() {
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        static STOP_FLAG: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(false);
[331](https://docs.rs#331)        let bg_thread = SharedThread::spawn(|| {
[332](https://docs.rs#332)            while !STOP_FLAG.load(Relaxed) {}
[333](https://docs.rs#333)            42
[334](https://docs.rs#334)        });
[335](https://docs.rs#335)        // Spawn 10 joiner threads that all simultaneously try to join the backgroud thread.
[336](https://docs.rs#336)        thread::scope(|scope| {
[337](https://docs.rs#337)            let mut joiner_handles = Vec::new();
[338](https://docs.rs#338)            for _ in 0..10 {
[339](https://docs.rs#339)                joiner_handles.push(scope.spawn(|| {
[340](https://docs.rs#340)                    bg_thread.join();
[341](https://docs.rs#341)                }));
[342](https://docs.rs#342)            }
[343](https://docs.rs#343)            // try_join will always return None here.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)            for _ in 0..100 {
[345](https://docs.rs#345)                assert!(bg_thread.try_join().is_none());
[346](https://docs.rs#346)                assert!(!bg_thread.is_finished());
[347](https://docs.rs#347)            }
[348](https://docs.rs#348)            STOP_FLAG.store(true, Relaxed);
[349](https://docs.rs#349)            // One of the joiner threads almost certainly has the underlying thread handle, and
[350](https://docs.rs#350)            // eventually it'll set SharedThread::result and one of these try_joins will return Some.
[351](https://docs.rs#351)            while !bg_thread.is_finished() {}
[352](https://docs.rs#352)            assert_eq!(bg_thread.try_join(), Some(&42));
[353](https://docs.rs#353)        });
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    }
[355](https://docs.rs#355)
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    #[test]
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    fn test_try_join_only() {
[358](https://docs.rs#358)        static STOP_FLAG: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(false);
[359](https://docs.rs#359)        let bg_thread = SharedThread::spawn(|| {
[360](https://docs.rs#360)            while !STOP_FLAG.load(Relaxed) {}
[361](https://docs.rs#361)            42
[362](https://docs.rs#362)        });
[363](https://docs.rs#363)        // try_join will always return None here.
[364](https://docs.rs#364)        for _ in 0..100 {
[365](https://docs.rs#365)            assert!(bg_thread.try_join().is_none());
[366](https://docs.rs#366)        }
[367](https://docs.rs#367)        STOP_FLAG.store(true, Relaxed);
[368](https://docs.rs#368)        // Eventually one of these try_join's will see .is_finished() = true and join the thread.
[369](https://docs.rs#369)        while bg_thread.try_join().is_none() {}
[370](https://docs.rs#370)        assert_eq!(bg_thread.try_join(), Some(&42));
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    }

[373](https://docs.rs#373)    #[test]
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    fn test_into_inner() {
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        let thread = SharedThread::spawn(|| String::from("foo"));
[376](https://docs.rs#376)        let result: String = thread.into_output();
[377](https://docs.rs#377)        assert_eq!(result, "foo");

# SharedThread in shared_thread - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/shared_thread/0.2.0/shared_thread/struct.SharedThread.html

`pub struct SharedThread<T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A wrapper around [ std::thread::JoinHandle](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/struct.JoinHandle.html) that allows for multiple waiters.

The high-level differences between `SharedThread` and [ JoinHandle](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/struct.JoinHandle.html) are:

- `join`- `&self`rather than- `&mut self`.
- `join`- `&T`rather than- `T`. For taking ownership of- `T`, see- `into_output`
- `SharedThread`also provides- `join_timeout`- `join_deadline`- `try_join`
- Rather than converting panics in into
`std::thread::Result``.unwrap()`every`.join()`,`SharedThread`propagates panics automatically.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use shared_thread::SharedThread;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering::Relaxed};
// Use this flag to tell our shared thread when to stop.
static EXIT_FLAG: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(false);
// Start a background thread that we'll share with several waiting threads.
let shared_thread = SharedThread::spawn(|| {
    // Pretend this is some expensive, useful background work...
    while (!EXIT_FLAG.load(Relaxed)) {}
    42
});
// It's up to you how to share the SharedThread object with other threads. In this sense it's
// like any other object you might need to share, like say a HashMap or a File. The common
// options are to put it in an Arc, or to let "scoped" threads borrow it directly. Let's use
// scoped threads.
std::thread::scope(|scope| {
    // Spawn three waiter threads that each wait on the shared thread.
    let waiter1 = scope.spawn(|| shared_thread.join());
    let waiter2 = scope.spawn(|| shared_thread.join());
    let waiter3 = scope.spawn(|| shared_thread.join());
    // In this example, the shared thread is going to keep looping until we set the EXIT_FLAG.
    // In the meantime, .is_finished() returns false, and .try_join() returns None.
    assert!(!shared_thread.is_finished());
    assert_eq!(shared_thread.try_join(), None);
    // Ask the shared thread to stop looping.
    EXIT_FLAG.store(true, Relaxed);
    // Now all the calls to .join() above will return quickly, and each of the waiter threads
    // will get a reference to the shared thread's output, &42.
    assert_eq!(*waiter1.join().unwrap(), 42);
    assert_eq!(*waiter2.join().unwrap(), 42);
    assert_eq!(*waiter3.join().unwrap(), 42);
    // Now that the shared thread has finished, .is_finished() returns true, and .try_join()
    // returns Some(&42).
    assert!(shared_thread.is_finished());
    assert_eq!(*shared_thread.try_join().unwrap(), 42);
});
 // We can take ownership of the output by consuming the SharedThread object. As with any
 // non-Copy type in Rust, this requires that the SharedThread is not borrowed.
 assert_eq!(shared_thread.into_output(), 42);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Wait for the shared thread to finish, then return `&T`. This blocks the current thread.

the first time. Subsequent calls panic with a generic message.

[93](https://docs.rs#93)// The shared thread sets this bool to true and signals the condvar when it exits, even if it
[94](https://docs.rs#94)// panicks.
[95](https://docs.rs#95)#[derive(Debug)]
[96](https://docs.rs#96)struct ExitSignal {
[97](https://docs.rs#97)    mutex: Mutex<bool>,
[98](https://docs.rs#98)    condvar: Condvar,
[99](https://docs.rs#99)}
[100](https://docs.rs#100)
[101](https://docs.rs#101)enum State<T> {
[102](https://docs.rs#102)    Running(thread::JoinHandle<T>),
[103](https://docs.rs#103)    // Note that the return value T goes in the OnceLock. If it lived here in the Exited variant,
[104](https://docs.rs#104)    // it would be stuck inside the state Mutex, and we couldn't share it with simple references.
[105](https://docs.rs#105)    Exited,
[106](https://docs.rs#106)    Panicked,
[107](https://docs.rs#107)}
[108](https://docs.rs#108)
[109](https://docs.rs#109)use State::*;

[111](https://docs.rs#111)impl<T> fmt::Debug for State<T> {
[112](https://docs.rs#112)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
[113](https://docs.rs#113)        match self {
[114](https://docs.rs#114)            Running { .. } => write!(f, "Running"),
[115](https://docs.rs#115)            Exited => write!(f, "Exited"),
[116](https://docs.rs#116)            Panicked => write!(f, "Panicked"),
[117](https://docs.rs#117)        }
[118](https://docs.rs#118)    }

[120](https://docs.rs#120)
[121](https://docs.rs#121)impl<T: Send + 'static> SharedThread<T> {
[122](https://docs.rs#122)    /// Spawn a new `SharedThread`.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    ///
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    /// # Panics
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    ///
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    /// This function calls
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    /// [`std::thread::spawn`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/fn.spawn.html) internally,
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    /// which panics if it fails to spawn a thread.
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    pub fn spawn<F>(f: F) -> Self
[130](https://docs.rs#130)    where
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        F: FnOnce() -> T + Send + 'static,
[132](https://docs.rs#132)    {
[133](https://docs.rs#133)        let exit_signal = Arc::new(ExitSignal {
[134](https://docs.rs#134)            mutex: Mutex::new(false),
[135](https://docs.rs#135)            condvar: Condvar::new(),
[136](https://docs.rs#136)        });
[137](https://docs.rs#137)        let exit_signal_clone = Arc::clone(&exit_signal);
[138](https://docs.rs#138)        let handle = thread::spawn(move || {
[139](https://docs.rs#139)            // Whether or not the closure `f` panics, set the exited flag and notify the condvar.
[140](https://docs.rs#140)            // It's not clear to me that the concept of "unwind safety" in the standard library was
[141](https://docs.rs#141)            // a good indea, but at least it doesn't require any unsafe code to work around it.
[142](https://docs.rs#142)            let unwind_result = catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(f));
[143](https://docs.rs#143)            let mut guard = lock_ignoring_poison(&exit_signal_clone.mutex);
[144](https://docs.rs#144)            *guard = true;
[145](https://docs.rs#145)            exit_signal_clone.condvar.notify_all();
[146](https://docs.rs#146)            // Now that we've signaled exit, if there was a panic, propagate it. The first waiter
[147](https://docs.rs#147)            // thread will observe it. (Subsequent waiter threads will only see the Panicked state
[148](https://docs.rs#148)            // variant.)
[149](https://docs.rs#149)            match unwind_result {
[150](https://docs.rs#150)                Ok(return_value) => return_value,
[151](https://docs.rs#151)                Err(panic) => resume_unwind(panic),
[152](https://docs.rs#152)            }
[153](https://docs.rs#153)        });
[154](https://docs.rs#154)        SharedThread {
[155](https://docs.rs#155)            state: Mutex::new(Running(handle)),
[156](https://docs.rs#156)            exit_signal,
[157](https://docs.rs#157)            output: OnceLock::new(),
[158](https://docs.rs#158)        }
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    }
[160](https://docs.rs#160)}
[161](https://docs.rs#161)
[162](https://docs.rs#162)// A thread that multiple other threads can wait on simultaneously.
[163](https://docs.rs#163)impl<T> SharedThread<T> {
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    fn join_exited_thread(&self, exit_signal_guard: MutexGuard<bool>) -> &T {
[165](https://docs.rs#165)        // It's not really important that we pass down the exit_signal_guard here, but it would
[166](https://docs.rs#166)        // probably live across this call anway, so it seems cleaner to take ownership of it.
[167](https://docs.rs#167)        debug_assert!(*exit_signal_guard, "the thread exited");
[168](https://docs.rs#168)
[169](https://docs.rs#169)        let mut state_guard = lock_ignoring_poison(&self.state);
[170](https://docs.rs#170)        match &*state_guard {
[171](https://docs.rs#171)            // Running means we're the thread that needs to .join(). Fall through.
[172](https://docs.rs#172)            Running(_) => {}
[173](https://docs.rs#173)            // Exited or Panicked means someone already joined.
[174](https://docs.rs#174)            Exited => return self.output.get().unwrap(),
[175](https://docs.rs#175)            Panicked => panic!("shared thread panicked"),
[176](https://docs.rs#176)        };
[177](https://docs.rs#177)
[178](https://docs.rs#178)        // We need to .join(), so take the JoinHandle by value. Use the Panicked state as a
[179](https://docs.rs#179)        // placeholder, so that it's the state we leave behind if something does in fact panic.
[180](https://docs.rs#180)        // This makes the Panicked state kind of ambiguous between "the other thread panicked" or
[181](https://docs.rs#181)        // "we failed an assert somewhere", but at least the initial panic backtrace will make it
[182](https://docs.rs#182)        // clear what happened.
[183](https://docs.rs#183)        let Running(handle) = mem::replace(&mut *state_guard, Panicked) else {
[184](https://docs.rs#184)            unreachable!()
[185](https://docs.rs#185)        };
[186](https://docs.rs#186)
[187](https://docs.rs#187)        // The thread has signaled that it's exiting, so .join() will return quickly. (It might
[188](https://docs.rs#188)        // block briefly it the thread is still cleaning itself up.) If it panicked, propagate the
[189](https://docs.rs#189)        // panic.
[190](https://docs.rs#190)        match handle.join() {
[191](https://docs.rs#191)            Ok(return_value) => {
[192](https://docs.rs#192)                // Because we set `output` while we hold the state mutex, it's guaranteed that
[193](https://docs.rs#193)                // subsequent threads that see the Exited state will also see that `output` is set.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)                let set_result = self.output.set(return_value);
[195](https://docs.rs#195)                assert!(set_result.is_ok(), "output must be previously unset");
[196](https://docs.rs#196)                *state_guard = Exited;
[197](https://docs.rs#197)                self.output.get().unwrap()
[198](https://docs.rs#198)            }
[199](https://docs.rs#199)            Err(panic) => resume_unwind(panic),
[200](https://docs.rs#200)        }
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    }
[202](https://docs.rs#202)
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    /// Wait for the shared thread to finish, then return `&T`. This blocks the current thread.
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    ///
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    /// # Panics
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    ///
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    /// This function panics if the shared thread panicked. The original panic is propagated
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    /// directly with [`resume_unwind`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/panic/fn.resume_unwind.html)
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    /// the first time. Subsequent calls panic with a generic message.
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    pub fn join(&self) -> &T {
[211](https://docs.rs#211)        let mut exit_signal_guard = lock_ignoring_poison(&self.exit_signal.mutex);
[212](https://docs.rs#212)        while !*exit_signal_guard {
[213](https://docs.rs#213)            exit_signal_guard = wait_ignoring_poison(&self.exit_signal.condvar, exit_signal_guard);
[214](https://docs.rs#214)        }
[215](https://docs.rs#215)        self.join_exited_thread(exit_signal_guard)
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    }
[217](https://docs.rs#217)
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    /// Wait with a timeout for the shared thread to finish. If it finishes in time (or it already
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    /// finished), return `Some(&T)`, otherwise return `None`. This blocks the current thread.
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    ///
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    /// # Panics
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    ///
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    /// This function panics if the shared thread panicked. The original panic is propagated
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// directly with [`resume_unwind`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/panic/fn.resume_unwind.html)
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    /// the first time it's observed. Subsequent calls panic with a generic message.
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    pub fn join_timeout(&self, timeout: Duration) -> Option<&T> {
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        let deadline = Instant::now() + timeout;
[228](https://docs.rs#228)        self.join_deadline(deadline)
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    }
[230](https://docs.rs#230)
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    /// Wait with a deadline for the shared thread to finish. If it finishes in time (or it already
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// finished), return `Some(&T)`, otherwise return `None`. This blocks the current thread.
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    ///
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    /// # Panics
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    ///
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    /// This function panics if the shared thread panicked. The original panic is propagated
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    /// directly with [`resume_unwind`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/panic/fn.resume_unwind.html)
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    /// the first time it's observed. Subsequent calls panic with a generic message.
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    pub fn join_deadline(&self, deadline: Instant) -> Option<&T> {
[240](https://docs.rs#240)        let mut exit_signal_guard = lock_ignoring_poison(&self.exit_signal.mutex);
[241](https://docs.rs#241)        while !*exit_signal_guard {
[242](https://docs.rs#242)            if Instant::now() > deadline {
[243](https://docs.rs#243)                return None;
[244](https://docs.rs#244)            }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)            exit_signal_guard = wait_deadline_ignoring_poison(
[246](https://docs.rs#246)                &self.exit_signal.condvar,
[247](https://docs.rs#247)                exit_signal_guard,
[248](https://docs.rs#248)                deadline,
[249](https://docs.rs#249)            );
[250](https://docs.rs#250)        }
[251](https://docs.rs#251)        Some(self.join_exited_thread(exit_signal_guard))
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    }
[253](https://docs.rs#253)
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    /// Return `Some(&T)` if the shared thread has already finished, otherwise `None`. This always
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    /// returns quickly.
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    ///
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    /// # Panics
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    ///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    /// This function panics if the shared thread panicked. The original panic is propagated
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    /// directly with [`resume_unwind`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/panic/fn.resume_unwind.html)
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    /// the first time it's observed. Subsequent calls panic with a generic message.
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    pub fn try_join(&self) -> Option<&T> {
[263](https://docs.rs#263)        let exit_signal_guard = lock_ignoring_poison(&self.exit_signal.mutex);
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        if *exit_signal_guard {
[265](https://docs.rs#265)            Some(self.join_exited_thread(exit_signal_guard))
[266](https://docs.rs#266)        } else {
[267](https://docs.rs#267)            None
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        }
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    }
[270](https://docs.rs#270)
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    /// Wait for the shared thread to finish, then return `T`. This blocks the current. This
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    /// requires ownership of the `SharedThread` and consumes it.
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    ///
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    /// # Panics
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    ///
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    /// This function panics if the shared thread panicked. The original panic is propagated
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// directly with [`resume_unwind`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/panic/fn.resume_unwind.html)
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    /// the first time it's observed. Subsequent calls panic with a generic message.
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    pub fn into_output(self) -> T {
[280](https://docs.rs#280)        self.join();
[281](https://docs.rs#281)        self.output.into_inner().expect("should be set")
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    }
[283](https://docs.rs#283)
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    /// Return `true` if the shared thread has finished, `false` otherwise.
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    ///
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    /// This function never blocks. If it returns `true`, [`try_join`][Self::try_join],
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    /// [`join_timeout`][Self::join_timeout], and [`join_deadline`][Self::join_deadline] are
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    /// guaranteed not to return `None`, and all join functions are guaranteed to return quickly.
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    pub fn is_finished(&self) -> bool {
[290](https://docs.rs#290)        *lock_ignoring_poison(&self.exit_signal.mutex)
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    }
[292](https://docs.rs#292)}
[293](https://docs.rs#293)
[294](https://docs.rs#294)fn lock_ignoring_poison<T>(mutex: &Mutex<T>) -> MutexGuard<'_, T> {
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    match mutex.lock() {
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        Ok(guard) => guard,
[297](https://docs.rs#297)        Err(e) => e.into_inner(),
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    }
[299](https://docs.rs#299)}
[300](https://docs.rs#300)
[301](https://docs.rs#301)fn wait_ignoring_poison<'guard, T>(
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    condvar: &Condvar,
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    guard: MutexGuard<'guard, T>,
[304](https://docs.rs#304)) -> MutexGuard<'guard, T> {
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    match condvar.wait(guard) {
[306](https://docs.rs#306)        Ok(guard) => guard,
[307](https://docs.rs#307)        Err(e) => e.into_inner(),
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    }
[309](https://docs.rs#309)}
[310](https://docs.rs#310)
[311](https://docs.rs#311)fn wait_deadline_ignoring_poison<'guard, T>(
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    condvar: &Condvar,
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    guard: MutexGuard<'guard, T>,
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    deadline: Instant,
[315](https://docs.rs#315)) -> MutexGuard<'guard, T> {
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    let timeout = deadline.saturating_duration_since(Instant::now());
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    match condvar.wait_timeout(guard, timeout) {
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        Ok((guard, _)) => guard,
[319](https://docs.rs#319)        Err(e) => e.into_inner().0,
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    }

# SharedThread in shared_thread - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/shared_thread/latest/target-redirect/shared_thread/struct.SharedThread.html

`pub struct SharedThread<T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A wrapper around [ std::thread::JoinHandle](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/struct.JoinHandle.html) that allows for multiple waiters.

The high-level differences between `SharedThread` and [ JoinHandle](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/struct.JoinHandle.html) are:

- `join`- `&self`rather than- `&mut self`.
- `join`- `&T`rather than- `T`. For taking ownership of- `T`, see- `into_output`
- `SharedThread`also provides- `join_timeout`- `join_deadline`- `try_join`
- Rather than converting panics in into
`std::thread::Result``.unwrap()`every`.join()`,`SharedThread`propagates panics automatically.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use shared_thread::SharedThread;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering::Relaxed};
// Use this flag to tell our shared thread when to stop.
static EXIT_FLAG: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(false);
// Start a background thread that we'll share with several waiting threads.
let shared_thread = SharedThread::spawn(|| {
    // Pretend this is some expensive, useful background work...
    while (!EXIT_FLAG.load(Relaxed)) {}
    42
});
// It's up to you how to share the SharedThread object with other threads. In this sense it's
// like any other object you might need to share, like say a HashMap or a File. The common
// options are to put it in an Arc, or to let "scoped" threads borrow it directly. Let's use
// scoped threads.
std::thread::scope(|scope| {
    // Spawn three waiter threads that each wait on the shared thread.
    let waiter1 = scope.spawn(|| shared_thread.join());
    let waiter2 = scope.spawn(|| shared_thread.join());
    let waiter3 = scope.spawn(|| shared_thread.join());
    // In this example, the shared thread is going to keep looping until we set the EXIT_FLAG.
    // In the meantime, .is_finished() returns false, and .try_join() returns None.
    assert!(!shared_thread.is_finished());
    assert_eq!(shared_thread.try_join(), None);
    // Ask the shared thread to stop looping.
    EXIT_FLAG.store(true, Relaxed);
    // Now all the calls to .join() above will return quickly, and each of the waiter threads
    // will get a reference to the shared thread's output, &42.
    assert_eq!(*waiter1.join().unwrap(), 42);
    assert_eq!(*waiter2.join().unwrap(), 42);
    assert_eq!(*waiter3.join().unwrap(), 42);
    // Now that the shared thread has finished, .is_finished() returns true, and .try_join()
    // returns Some(&42).
    assert!(shared_thread.is_finished());
    assert_eq!(*shared_thread.try_join().unwrap(), 42);
});
 // We can take ownership of the output by consuming the SharedThread object. As with any
 // non-Copy type in Rust, this requires that the SharedThread is not borrowed.
 assert_eq!(shared_thread.into_output(), 42);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Wait for the shared thread to finish, then return `&T`. This blocks the current thread.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

This function panics if the shared thread panicked. The original panic is propagated
directly with [ resume_unwind](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/panic/fn.resume_unwind.html)
the first time. Subsequent calls panic with a generic message.

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

CLI Helpers
